record.paper_title: Open Problems on Graph Coloring for Special Graph Classes
record.original_question: For a graph G = (V, E), the Coloring problem asks whether G has a coloring with at most k colors, where a coloring assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different colors. A graph is even-cycle-free if it has no induced cycle of even length, and it is even-anticycle-free if it has no induced subgraph that is the complement of an even cycle. What is the computational complexity of Coloring when the input is restricted to even-cycle-free graphs, and what is the computational complexity of Coloring when the input is restricted to even-anticycle-free graphs?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 1 Determine the complexity of Coloring for even-cycle-free graphs and even-anticycle-free graphs.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple undirected graph. A (proper) coloring of G is an assignment of colors to the vertices of G such that no two adjacent vertices receive the same color. For an integer k ≥ 1, the Coloring problem takes as input a graph G and an integer k, and asks whether G admits a proper coloring using at most k colors.

An induced cycle in G is a cycle whose vertex set induces, in G, exactly the edges of that cycle (a chordless cycle). Call a graph even-cycle-free if it contains no induced cycle of even length, and even-anticycle-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to the complement of an even-length cycle.

Determine the computational complexity (e.g., polynomial-time solvable, NP-complete, or otherwise) of the Coloring problem in each of the following two cases:
(a) the input graph G is restricted to be even-cycle-free;
(b) the input graph G is restricted to be even-anticycle-free.
artifact.status_search_result: The complexity of Coloring restricted to even-cycle-free graphs and even-anticycle-free graphs is described as a long-standing open problem. While the analogous problems for odd-cycle-free (bipartite) and odd-anticycle-free (cobipartite) graphs are polynomial-time solvable, switching the parity from odd to even yields two open complexity questions that remain unresolved.
